EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Winds behind yet another arctic front reached speeds from 30 to 45 mph with gusts as high as 55 to 65 mph across southwest Minnesota. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds were sustained from 40 to 42 mph with gusts as high as 64 mph near Beaver Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A push of dangerously cold air spread across the Upper Midwest behind a series of strong arctic fronts from January 21 through January 23. Wind chills dropped into the -40s across much of the region, with AXN in Alexandria reporting the coldest wind chill of -50F during this stretch of extreme cold. EVENT_NARRATIVE: KANE reported wind gusts as high as 25 mph during the early evening as air temperatures dropped from -15F to -20F overnight. The lowest measured wind chill was -44F at 2AM on the 23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A second wave of wintry precipitation occurred 24 hours after a light mix of snow and freezing rain fell the day prior. This round was heavier and temperatures were right around freezing, leading to a mixture of freezing rain and rain. By the morning commute, most areas saw more of a crunchy slush on the ground as the heavier rain started to melt the coating of ice that developed overnight. The heaviest impacted area was western Hennepin, Wright, Anoka, and Chisago counties where temperatures were slightly cooler and the rain rates were not as heavy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS at KHCD reported several hours of freezing precipitation starting during the evening of January 5th and lasting into the early morning of the 6th. CoCoRaHS observers reported freezing rain and ice covered sidewalks near Hutchinson and Glencoe.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stacked surface low was located over northeastern MN. An area of deformation developed across the Dakotas and moved slowly into Minnesota. Forcing within the mid-levels allowed for moderate to heavy snow to fall across western MN. Additionally, due to the strength of the pressure gradient, wind gusts across much of western MN ranged between 35 to 50 mph. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure developed across the High Plains on the 17th and moved across the Dakotas on the 18th and into northern Wisconsin on the morning of the 19th. This led to a prolonged period of snowfall across the region. The track of this low was favorable for lake and terrain enhancement along the North Shore. Additionally, the strong low led to very gusty winds along the North Shore that led to a prolonged period of blizzard conditions that led to the closure of Minnesota Highway 61 for about 3 hours as crews were unable to keep up with the snowfall. Snowfall accumulations inland of Lake Superior were 6 to 10 inch range with much higher amounts along the North Shore, including upwards of 40 inches for the event in Hovland right on the shore of Lake Superior.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snowfall and strong winds led to an 11 hour period of blizzard conditions along the North Shore on the 18th. Minnesota Highway 61 was closed to traffic for about 3 hours from Duluth to the Canadian Border as road crews were unable to keep up with the snow. Snowfall totals well over 2 feet were reported with a high report of 40.4 inches at Hovland for the event.

The initial area of light snow ended during the early morning of January 18 as a strong cold front moved into the region. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weather system resulted in a light wintry mix of precipitation during the early afternoon on January 4th. Surface temperatures were about 5 to 10 degrees below freezing, under a slightly warmer air mass just above the surface. This resulted in a few hours of light freezing rain or drizzle, and ultimately light ice accretion, creating slick surfaces for a number of counties in east-central Minnesota. Farther north, the airmass just above the surface was slightly cooler, resulting in more snow mixing in with any freezing precipitation. This limited impacts for areas north and west of St Cloud, Princeton, and Rush City.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS at KSYN reported an hour of a mixture of light freezing precipitation during the afternoon. CoCoRaHS observers reported a light mixture of sleet, freezing rain, and rain in Cannon Falls and Nerstrand.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A second wave of wintry precipitation occurred 24 hours after a light mix of snow and freezing rain fell the day prior. This round was heavier and temperatures were right around freezing, leading to a mixture of freezing rain and rain. For most locations, the main period of freezing occurred overnight from the 5th into the 6th as rainfall rates were lighter. Rates then increased during the morning of the 6th which made it difficult for ice accretion to continue as temperatures hovered right around the freezing point. By the morning commute, most areas saw more of a crunchy slush on the ground as the heavier rain started to melt the coating of ice that developed overnight. The heaviest impacted area was western Hennepin, Wright, Anoka, and Chisago counties where temperatures were slightly cooler and the rain rates were not as heavy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS at KMKT reported several hours of freezing precipitation during the evening of January 5th. Several CoCoRaHS observers reported freezing rain and ice covered sidewalks and driveways near Mankato, Lake Crystal, and Minnesota Lake.

A strong upper trough moved across the Northern Plains and into northwest Minnesota, bringing strong winds, light snow, and blizzard conditions. The initial area of light snow ended during the early morning of January 18 as a strong cold front moved into the region. Post frontal snow showers along with strong winds behind the front contributed to widespread whiteout conditions primarily across northeast North Dakota and the Red River Valley of northwest Minnesota. Strongest wind gusts were 50 to 57 mph. A no travel advised was issued by MNDOT in far northwest Minnesota due to whiteout conditions.
